utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber would like to turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll just wait until Madam Usher has removed also the other ... Then I will also call you by your own name since the application for protective measures have been withdrawn, Mr. Kardum. You gave already your solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth in closed session. You are still bound by that declaration and you will now first be examined by Mr. Margetts, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kardum. Mr. Kardum, could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am Ive Kardum. I was born in 1957 in a place called Nunic, the Kistanje municipality, not far from Zadar. I now live in Zadar and I work in the police administration of Zadar. Otherwise, as far as my basic education goes, I am professor of philosophy and archeology. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, first of all, please remain seated. You might spend quite a number of hours in this court and there's no need -- just remain seated. Could you also focus very much on the questions that are put to you. For example, at this moment, Mr. Margetts only asked for your full name. Of course, if Mr. Margetts would like to pay further attention to your education, and your present position, he will certainly ask about that. But for the -- please focus your answer first to what has been asked. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 23rd of March, 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if 65 ter 5273 could please be brought up on the screen. And if I may provide Mr. Kardum with a hard copy of this document. At this moment, Mr. President, I would just like to indicate that Mr. Kardum has not had the opportunity to review these statements subsequent to the statements having been given and then a further meeting that was held with the Office of the Prosecutor last year, so he has not had an opportunity recently to review the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kardum, could you please look at that statement. Is that the statement that you gave on the 23rd of March, 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave a statement on the 23rd of March, 2004, in Zagreb. I don't understand English. I gave the statement in Croatian. The questions were in English, and those questions were translated into Croatian. I answered in Croatian. The statement was read back to me in the English [as interpreted] language. I had quite a number of queries about the translation of what I said. I asked to be supplied with the statement but I was told that the rules are such that I couldn't be given the statement either in English or in Croatian. I wasn't satisfied with that decision. However, I respected the rules and I signed the statement. Now, whether this statement fully complies with what I said, in terms of translation, it's difficult to say. As far as I see now, there are 13 pages to this statement. Now, if there's time I'd like to go through the statement again or at least the portions that I consider to be more significant. I didn't have any criticisms with respect to the way the interview was conducted and the questions but my criticism was about the translations, interpretations and so on and so forth, and what was signed on not. I don't know whether what I said in Croatian was translated in exactly the same way as I said it in the English version. But, yes, this is my signature on the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the witness's answers, it seems to me that he may need an opportunity to review the translation of this statement he is referring to. I'd also like to refer him to another document before he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first inquire, do I understand that you do read and understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statement was read back to you in English, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement was written in English and then the interpreter read it out to me in Croatian so this is a second-hand or third-hand translation because it's -- the statement is given in Croatian, it is translated into English, then the translator reads it out but translates it back to me in Croatian and then I sign the statement in English. So I did sign it but I did have criticisms and queries with respect to the translation and the way in which it was translated and interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only reason why I asked is because earlier it was -- we find on our transcript that the statement was read back to you in English but I now understand that it was read back to you from the English -- English language by an interpreter who interpreted into Croatian. That also clarifies the issue why you may have had queries as far as the interpretation is concerned. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, did you also meet last year with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and did you give another statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 4th of May, 2007?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to the investigator of the International Tribunal. You personally, in fact. Mr. Foster and you, yourself. You talked to me on the 3rd or 4th of May, 2007. I have no criticisms with respect to that statement of mine except to say that I made it in what was for me a very difficult time. That is to say, when my father was dying in hospital and he did, in fact, die five days later. So that day, I missed my opportunity to talk to him for the last time. That opportunity was not given to me anymore before he died. Now, I don't have any criticisms to make of you or Mr. Foster because I didn't insist. Had I insisted I am sure you would have postponed the interview for some other time, to respond to my request. So I don't hold it against you but I'd just like to mention it in passing. The interview was heard in a proper manner. As far as translation and interpretation goes, the same holds true for what I said a moment ago and we had even more misunderstandings and queries with respect to the translation. I'm sure you will remember that there are quite a lot of things that were said in English that could not be properly translated into Croatian, and I explained to you that in Croatian that translation and that word meant something quite a bit different to what it did in English. So I will draw your attention to some of those things. Whether you managed to explain them properly and get them put right, we'll see in due course. But, anyway thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if you could please bring up 65 ter 5274 on to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, I would just like to express my condolences to you in respect of the death of your father. Obviously we were not aware of the situation at the time we were meeting with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, could you look at the left-hand side of the screen. Is that a copy of the statement that you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I may provide a hard copy of the statement to the witness, hard copy of the translation, statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, at first glance that should be it. Although the statement is quite a lengthy one so I can't go into the contents now. We can do that later on through your questions, of course. I have never seen my statement in this shape and form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That's a translation of the English statement that you provided to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in light of the witness's responses, we'd like to give the witness an opportunity to read through his previous statements. We've already handed to him the two statements in the Croatian language and we also have the numerous documents that were referred to particularly in the second statement in a binder, also in Croatian. If we could hand that to him as well and possibly we could give an opportunity to him to review those materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to do that right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think if we're to proceed with 92 ter procedure which I still think is a profitable one, and ultimately would save us time, then it may be helpful if we do take a short break and give the witness possibly 30 to 40 minutes to consider these documents. And, Your Honour, I regret that we were unable to meet with him in the last few days. We had scheduled a proofing session yesterday and earlier today and Mr. Kardum deemed it appropriate to decline our suggestion in relation to that procedure and that's the reason that we find ourselves in the position we're in now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, one of the problems is that if we would take a break now that we would need three breaks today, which would be an additional loss of time. Is there any way, Mr. Margetts, that you could choose portions of your examination which are least likely to sufficient from any translation issues, that we could, for example, continue for another half an hour, three quarters of an hour and then give an opportunity to the witness to read and meanwhile we would then have these statements marked for identification and that if, of course, the witness -- if parts of the statement are put to him, would like to comment on it, he'll have an opportunity to do so, but after that, we would then invite him to read through the whole of the statements. Is that a -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I'd like to emphasise that if you say, no, I could not put any question to the witness under those -- on this basis, as suggested by me, then of course the Chamber will most likely follow your suggestion. But it is a kind of a solution which would not result in a loss of time and, at the same time, to some extent will meet your concerns and, of course, also the Chamber's concerns. And before we proceed of course I should also give an opportunity to the Defence to -- to comment, if there's any need to do so, on the suggested way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Maybe, Mr. President, just before the Defence do comment I can put forward alternative scenarios in terms of how the examination will proceed. I certainly accept Your Honour's suggestion that we proceed with the examination and I will do it in a form that's acceptable. The examination -- examination-in-chief was intended to build upon the statements and the -- in fact, I don't think there would have been I would have asked that didn't first refer the witness back to paragraphs of his statement. So I'm interested to know from the Defence whether that procedure is something that -- that they're happy with me proceeding with in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then may I take it that then the first question always to the witness would be, Is this what you intended to say, does this reflect what you said and then have follow-up questions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the portions dealt with would then be verified at this very moment and would then give an opportunity to the witness later to finish reading the whole of the -- of the statement. That's your suggestion. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was going to be my suggestion as well. That's fine with us. And as a matter of fact, I, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, would prefer that because in light of certain things that happened with -- not last witness but the penultimate witness, and the statement, I would just as soon that the witness be given as much time as he needs to go through the statements so we don't have any questions later about why changes were or were not made to the statement. And if light of that, if Mr. Margetts wants to go through his direct and just refer to the portions, ask him if he still agrees with the statement, then I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kardum, we'll proceed in the following way. Mr. Margetts will start with his examination-in-chief. He may refer to portions of your statements. He will first give you an opportunity to read that relevant part of your statement and then put further questions to you. But during the first break - and then please indicate how much time would you need - you're invited to go through the whole of your two statements and to see where you'd like to make amendments specifically in view of the -- of the observations you made in relation to the translation of your statements. That's how we'll proceed. Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one other practical matter and that is that the parties have reviewed the 92 ter submission, obviously, and have assented effectively with some corrections from the Cermak team in relation to the statements and the documents annexed thereto pending, of course, the 92 ter procedure being successfully completed. Nevertheless, in respect of the documents which are quite an extensive list of documents, some 33 documents, I don't know whether the parties would be happy for those to be moved into evidence at this stage and be given exhibit numbers. That may be an efficient way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this point I think I would prefer to hear what the witness has to say about a particular document before we agree to move it into evidence. The 92 ter, our agreement to it obviously is always contingent what the witness will say in court as to the procedure under Rule 92 ter. And in light of that, I think, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, we would first like to hear what the witness has to say about his statements before we start move -- start moving documents into evidence unless on direct he is going to authenticate documents and otherwise provide foundation for their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then of course another alternative would be if, for whatever reason, this would not be an appropriate way of introducing these documents into evidence, that of course the Prosecution could still consider to tender them from the bar table if it -- if that could be appropriately done. So all alternatives would be open if the introduction of these documents through the witness would not be the appropriate one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, first I'd like to deal with some formal matters relating to your role, specifically in the period from August 1995 and the various procedures that were adopted in the Zadar-Knin criminal police department. And I'd first like to refer to you to a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 3200 presented on the screen, and we could move to page 7 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. Mr. Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have 3200 on the exhibit list disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last one it appears under number 8, but I must admit that I had quite a busy mourning in replacing one exhibit list by the more recent one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The most recent one I have is number 8. As of 1.00 p.m. today number 8 is 2999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm confronted with a curious situation that the documents that the Registrar is bringing up on the screen is the correct document, but I'm informed that the number should be 2999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're right, Mr. Misetic. I took one of the wrong ones of this morning. I now have the one which is not stapled. It's the last one. Mr. Margetts, is 3200 still on your exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It seems to me that 3200 is a duplicate of 2999. I think if we go with 2999 that may be the best way to proceed. So, Mr. Registrar, if we could bring up 65 ter 2999, please, and we could move to page 7 of the English and we could move to page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you'll on the right-hand side of your screen that the document that appears is a report in respect of events that took place on the liberated territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if, Mr. Registrar, you could move to the second page of this document. Sorry, not the second page. And if we could move back again to page 4 of the document on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, you will see in the listing here that there is a reference to the police administrations of the various areas, including the police administration in Sisak-Moslavina, Karlovac, Split-Dalmatia and then a reference to Zadar-Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page, please, Mr. Registrar. And one page further on the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, you'll see on the B/C/S version there is a listing of police stations in the Knin district, Kotar-Knin. And you'll see there's a reference to Knin, Donji Lapac, Gracac, Lovinac, Korenica, Benkovac, and Obrovac. Are they the police stations that the crime police were stationed at in August 1995 and was there a crime department at each of these stations; or if there was not a crime department at each of these police stations, could you please indicate which one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the organisational chart that was developed earlier, I don't know exactly when, perhaps 1991, 1992, or 1993, I wouldn't know the exact year, but I know that the Zadar-Knin police administration was established as such in 1993. Before that, the area of Knin was part of the Sibenik police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let me stop you. You are telling us, in quite some detail, how matters developed over the years. However, the question was whether, in the listed police stations, whether there was a crime police section and if so, which one; or if not in which ones not. That's the question. And we are under some time restraints so we have to focus on what Mr. Margetts asks you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the organisational chart, they should have had crime police departments. However, in August of -- in the month of August, they did not have that. Not one of these police stations had a crime department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, could you indicate when the crime departments were formed and these police stations did have crime departments, if all of them did, or if any of them didn't, please indicate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to an internal arrangement, the criminal policemen -- the first criminal policemen who were to carry out crime investigations within these police stations were sent out toward the end of August or in early September 1995. There were some four or five criminal policemen who were sent to Knin to cover the area of the police -- of the Knin police station. Four or five police officers were sent to Benkovac to cover the Benkovac-Obrovac and Stankovci area and four or five police officers, criminal police officers were sent to Gracac to cover the area of Lika which was part of the Zadar-Knin. In other words, Gracac -- covering Gracac, Korenica and Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in respect of the Obrovac area, were criminal police sent to the Obrovac police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Obrovac was covered by the crime police from Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And specifically in regard to Lovinac, were criminal police sent to Lovinac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lovinac is a part of Lika and this area was covered by the crime police from Gracac. That police station in Lovinac, I think, even under the organisational chart, it was not supposed to have a crime police department. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. If we could move on to another related topic and that is, as the chief of the crime police in the Zadar-Knin police administration, who were your superiors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My superiors in Zadar were the deputy chief of the police administration. Do you want me to tell you what his name was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is Mr. Nedjeljko Pavlovic and the chief of the police administration, Mr. Ivica Cetina. At the level of the police administration, the further jurisdiction was with the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And the chiefs of the criminal police in Zagreb, who were your superiors, what were their names and what were their positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Zagreb my direct superior was the chief of the crime police sector, Mr. Ivan Nadj, and at the apex of this pyramid in was Mr. Marijan Benko. In addition to these, there were some six to seven chiefs of departments in Zagreb, they were assistants to Mr. Nadj and they were, in a certain sense, just in the areas of their expertise they were my superiors. This whole group was headed by Mr. Nadj who was my first or direct immediate superior in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, just to move on again and to deal with some more structural or procedural matters, could you describe to the Trial Chamber the way in which events that take place in and around the area of the police stations are recorded. For example, is there a log of daily events that the operations officer compiles, and also if you could explain how crimes are recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Incidents were recorded at the level of the police station. That was the first step. For instance, if there was an event -- an incident in Knin -- in -- it should have been recorded at the police station in Knin. That was the first step. It would be entered in the log-book of daily incidents, which is compiled at the operations centre of the police station in Knin. This log-book contains a column which describes who reported the event, whether it was a civilian or a citizen, a police, a police officer, a soldier, the name of the person and so forth. Then the next entry would be the event itself and a short description of the incident. And following that, there would be a column stating who was informed of the event and what steps were taken to address it. Further on, these events were supposed to - although I didn't really see this - but they were supposed to be recorded also in the log-book of the police administration of the Knin district, and following this, also in the log-book of the police administration for Zadar-Knin, within the operations duty service. I have to stress that all these operations centres or operations duty services were part of the military department at the level of -- at the police department at the level of the police administration in Knin-Kotar. Further on what happens after that, I wouldn't know whether they are registered at the ministry itself or not, I wouldn't know about that portion. As for criminal logs, they were compiled in the same manner that they are today, only at the level of police stations. There is no department for police and no ministry. The crime log-books were only compiled by the police stations. That's how it was done in the past and that's how it is still done today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And could you please explain to the Court how it is that an entry comes to be made in the crime log or the crime register.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When an incident is assessed as a criminal offence, then it would be assigned a K or a Q number. Some people would read this as K or as Q. So K number, for instance, K 95/ -- 25/95. This, for instance, would refer to a criminal event that occurred on a certain day and that is registered as criminal offence K 25/95. Then there would be also mention of what exactly happened, whether the perpetrator is known or not. Who reported it, what type of crime offence this is, whether it's a robbery or an armed robbery and also the date of when the -- the event was reported would be entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You state at the commencement of your answer, "When an incident is assessed as a criminal offence," who makes that assessment and refers it to the criminal operations officer for entry into the register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually this would be entered by the assistant chief at the police station and he would assign this number. But this can also be done by the duty officer at the police station if it is agreed with the district attorney that this is how it should be. So, if this event was referred to the district attorney, then it -- he may suggest, put forward a suggestion of how to qualify this event. Then it would also depend on when this was reported whether it was during the working hours or outside of the working hours, whether the offence was reported during the weekend and so forth. So that's how it was determined what a crime would be assessed as or what kind of qualification would be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So entry in the criminal register would be the first information criminal police received in relation to that crime having taken place and the investigative steps would follow from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this was not the first time that it would be recorded. The first record would be made within the system of the Ministry of the Interior, where it would be entered in the computer system. However, at this time, this was just a fledgeling system and it was not as good as it is today. Today every event or every incident is recorded and entered in the computer system and we can see what is all the events. However, at this time this was done regularly because there was no electric power and we had other difficulties in trying to make the whole system work. So the first information would reach the duty service and the duty service would enter or register this in the information system. Just a brief information --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I apologise for interrupting you but my question was actually as to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure the witness answered my question. If we look at page --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm listening to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was listening to him in the original language and he was getting to the point of -- he was in the middle of explaining the reporting from the operative centre. So I'd ask that he be allowed to finish that thought because I do think it is responsive to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it takes him so many lines then I should perhaps again stress that you should focus your answer immediately on the question put to you. There was some disagreement or whether you slowly came to that point or you had not arrived yet at that point. Could I ask you again to focus your answers precisely on what was asked of you. The question that was put to you, Mr. Kardum, was the following, and -- Mr. Margetts said: "So the entry in the criminal register would be the first information criminal police received in relation to that crime having taken place and the investigative steps would follow from there?" That was the question. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And if I could be of guidance to the witness, I think the difference between the question and the answer was the reference to the criminal police receiving information, rather than operations officers or others receiving information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question, focussing on the criminal police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I already answered my question with all my previous answers. But I will repeat. Everything that happens in the field will first reach the duty service. The duty service would then register it in the log-book and I've already described how some of these entries were made. I mentioned how the computer system was still in its pioneering stages at that time. We didn't have sufficient computers, a sufficient number of computers to enter all of that like that. So, all the events that would transpire over a period of 24 hours would then be compiled in a piece of information, or an information sheet. This information sheet would be in the file of the head of the department and one such information sheet would also reach me and also the -- the chiefs of all departments, so we would all receive the same information sheet and the first thing we would do when arrived to work in the morning would be to read this information sheet. If there were any events in it that were of special significance, then after 30 minutes or an hour we would be informed by the duty service if this was what the duty operations officer considered necessary to inform the chief of section, the deputy chief and the head of the crime police. Then the duty officer would inform these people of such information as soon as he received it and in the log-book he would enter all the names of individuals who had been informed of it. For instance, if there was a robbery, or some serious crime that was committed, or a major accident, traffic accident, the duty officer would inform immediately the chief of police, the crime -- the head of the crime department, and the assistants. So those are the individuals that were informed and if --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would just like you to explain to the Court the significance of the crime register and the extent to which the incidents of crime were recorded in that log-book.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was no special significance of it. This is more for statistical purposes so that we can review when we prepare our annual reports. We wanted to make sure that we always had a written document, what items were resolved, which ones weren't, so there was no special significance other than that. And I apologise, I did not hear your -- the second part of your question. I only answered about the significance of this log-book, but I was unable to answer the second part of your question, because I -- I don't recall your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kardum. The question is the extent to which the criminal events that took place in the areas covered by the police stations were entered into the crime registers, to what extent were the crimes recorded in those crime registers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a rule, everything should be entered in the registers. However, I assume that you want to know whether this was being done in this new police stations that were established. I really can't answer that question because I have never seen them, and the system of the crime police, the organisation of the crime police, was rather lagging behind our work, so I believe that in the beginning it wasn't even kept. These registers weren't even kept. We from the police administration often helped police stations in this area in their daily work, and I'm not sure that all the events from that time were actually registered in the crime registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if they weren't registered in the crime registers, where would have they been registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think there was any other place where they would have been registered. They would have been sent to the district attorney. Every criminal offence or every file case that was assigned a K number would be then forwarded to the appropriate prosecutor, the district attorney. We used to call it prosecutor; now we call it district attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'm sorry to ask so many questions about this issue and I definitely will move on. But in your last answer you referred to the assignment of a K number and going back to your earlier answer when that took place, is it not the case that the K numbers are assigned and recorded in the crime registers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are registered in the crime register. However, I believe that not all the numbers from that period were actually entered in the crime register. I have to be honest, I never actually reviewed these registers at the police stations so I can't be sure. It is quite possible there are far more Q numbers than you can find in registers. In other words, that the police actually handled and investigated more cases than it actually entered at the time in the crime registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Kardum. I'd now like to move on to another related topic, and that is: In August 1995, how many men did you have subordinated to you in the crime police department of the Zadar-Knin administration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not going to give you the correct figure, but I would say between 50 and 60. 50 and 60 people. And in the crime police department I had a number of sections. If you recall, it was one of the things we didn't agree upon with the translation from Croatian into English and vice versa. I always told you that I was chief of the crime department whereas you called me a sector. A sector is something higher than a department. For example, if you have a company that numbers 180, you call the person in charge, the commander in charge, a battalion commander which has many more men. So anyway, 50 to 60 people divided in a number of departments or sections. One was the crime technology department. They were employees in the crime department. They all had secondary school training except for the leader of the department who had university training. Then I had seven or eight people in the commercial crime -- economic crime sector and they also had university training, usually the faculty of economics or graduates from the factual of law. Then I had three or four men working in the drugs department, drug section, and they had secondary school education. Then another department was for organised crime and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I stop you there. On the second line of your answer you said already 50 to 60 people, then you started referring, which is fine, to terminology that was used during the interview but now we are at the academic qualifications, something that really was not asked for. Mr. Kardum, may I again ask you to focus on what is asked. And, Mr. Margetts, of course you're examining the witness. You will certainly find a fair balance between interrupting and not interrupting but whether you have found it already is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will be mindful of your guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, in addition to the 50 to 60 people you described located at the Zadar-Knin police administration, how many crime police investigators would have you had to deploy at the police stations that we referred to earlier, Benkovac, Gracac, Obrovac, and the other stations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just add one sentence with respect to the people in the crime police department. Usually they were workers who had had about two years experience of working in the police force. So they were inexperienced young people, in actual fact, who had not gained a great deal of experience working in the police force and especially in the crime police. I see that you don't have time for me to explain the reasons for that but I'd just like to say one sentence and that is this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'll let you just say that sentence, it's just that I'm going to ask very specific questions. If you could give me short answers then I can ask follow-up questions. But my specific enquiry is the number of people apart from those employed at Zadar-Knin police administration, the number of crime investigators that were in the field at the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already given you that answer. If you followed what I said, I said that there were four or five of them who were sent to Knin sometime towards the end of August or beginning of September and the same number in Benkovac for the Benkovac-Obrovac area and Stankovci as well and also four or five to the Gracac for the area there, Gracac, Lapac and Korenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for -- I'm sorry to interrupt. Just for clarification, in the question it was posed as if these are people in addition to the 50 to 60 that he identified or is it to ask of the 50 to 60, how many were sent to the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. The question was intended to ask in addition to the 50 to 60 in the Zadar-Knin police administration, how many investigators were located at the police stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question would be whether those located at the police stations were among the 50 or 60 or in addition to the 50 or 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the ones you said were sent to the various police stations, were they in addition to the 50 or 60 or are they included in the 50 or 60 people that were subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, they were people whom I sent from my department. So I sent them from my Zadar department or from the first police or second police station in Zadar. So they weren't people added to that number. They were people taken from that number. So when I asked you [as interpreted] how many people I had subordinated to me, I gave you the answer for the total number of men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So my relatively simple question could have been answered by, no, they were among the 50 or 60 I told you about. That would have given the full information which the question apparently seeks. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'd now like to turn my attention to the activities of the criminal police from the 5th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if I could, please, have, Mr. Registrar, on the screen 65 ter 5278, which is at tab 22 in the exhibits, if that's of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, you see on the right-hand side of the screen there a list. Is this list familiar to you; and if so, could you explain to the Court what this list represents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is a list of individuals who were taken in, in the collection centre for prisoners of war in Zadar. And the first among them is Rade Pupovac. So that's a list that was compiled in hand because we still hadn't set up a system by which all this information could be typed out and so on. I'd like to mention this first case, Rade Pupovac, his father's name, his date of birth, the 24th of May in 1956, the place is Biljane, nationality Croatian, when taken over by the crime police at 1845 hours on the 5th of August. When he left at 1030 on the 9th of August, 1995, he was escorted by a police employee Josip Vrancic, and he was handed over to the investigation centre and it doesn't say which court but probably the court in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you referred to the nationality. Does the reference to Croatian refer to citizenship or does it refer to nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is citizenship. Rade Pupovac, as far as I know, was a Serb by ethnicity. His father's name is Jovan. So I can judge by the names. Anyway, he was an ethnic Serb but a citizen of the state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And these individuals who were detained or held at the prisoner of war facility in Zadar, predominantly what was their nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are all not all prisoners of war. Some of these people -- well, it turned out that many of them had not taken part in the armed struggle against the Republic of Croatia, because we're dealing with an armed struggle, and they were released straight away. So in the column to whom they were turned over to, it would say the collection centre for civilians. Anyway, these people were mostly Serbs but among them there were some Croats as well. I see Simet [phoen] Petrov here, that name. He is a Croat and there are probably other examples, just looking down the list. So there were Croats there as well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'll refer to you a report in a moment. I would just like to take you through two further documents before I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please have up on the screen 65 ter 5238 [Realtime transcript read in error "5328"].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you see on the screen in front of you, on the right-hand side, a -- a cover letter enclosing an outline of a structure of a final report in relation to the treatment of the prisoners of war and it is dated 16 August 1995 and is from Ivan Nadj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please just turn over the pages of this particular instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Kardum, is this instruction familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was compiled in the Ministry of the Interior. Mr. Ivan Nadj, the chief of the sector of crime police, sent this to all the police departments that were engulfed by Operation Storm, whether it was Sector South or Sector North, and they were sent out a document setting out what happened to the prisoners of war, how many of them we had, how many of them were processed, where they ended up --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- other structures and elements and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. I'd like to now refer you to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that's, Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 5026.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just for the record, I see on the transcript 5328 and it's 5238.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just about to correct that one way or the other. I don't know whether it's just the transcript or whether said that, Mr. Margetts, but apparently the registrar was able to get 5238 on the screen, but I'll check whether that's the number assigned to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, that's 65 ter 5238.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. And, yes, if, Mr. Registrar, we could now have 5026, 65 ter. Mr. Registrar, I believe we still have 5238 on the screen. If it is of any assistance, it's tab 19 of the exhibit list, 16 August order from Mr. Ive Kardum. Unfortunately, that's the same document. So I may just indicate to Mr. Kardum that we'll endeavour to rectify the problem we have here and in the interim if I could pass to Mr. Kardum a hard copy of this document, and for the parties' reference, it's the document referenced at number 19 of the -- of the exhibit list. And I don't know whether ... it's a very brief document, Your Honours, and I'll hand up a copy to the Court in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, could it be put on the ELMO. One copy for three Judges is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll look at it on the ELMO. Well, the witness can look at the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have looked at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, and this is a letter forwarded by you enclosing Mr. Nadj's instructions and requesting the preparation and compilation of the information that Mr. Nadj sought. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if we could look at the names of the people who are listed here, there are the names of six persons and I believe that these individuals are the leaders of the various departments that you -- that were subordinated to you in the Zadar-Knin police administration. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that would be that the analytical department chiefs and deputies are listed from the second person to the sixth person and the first individual is the commander of the holding centre for prisoners of war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. That's not correct. May I explain and go through the individuals one by one. Adem Mehmedovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- was subordinate to me up until Operation Storm and he was chief of the general crimes department. On the day of Operation Storm, pursuant to an order from the chief of the police administration, he was appointed the chief of the holding centre for prisoners of war in Zadar. By the same token, he was an individual who was no longer subordinated to me but directly to the chief of the police administration. So he was the commander of this holding centre for prisoners of war. In actual fact, at the time I actually lost one man from the crime police, and he was a key individual from the general crime department because he was an experienced policeman. I don't know whether the chief of the police administration liked the fact that he was a Bosniak and chose him for that reason to appoint him commander but let's leave that alone for the time being. Anyway, on to the next one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'll just ask you a series of short questions. How many crime police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked the witness first to go to -- he offered to go through the list. Skrgetic, was he head of the analytical department of the Zadar-Knin and was he subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. She was on a par with me and she was chief of another department and she was subordinated, just like me, to the chief of the police administration, the deputy and the chief of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next one on the list, Mikulic, same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ante Mikulic was my subordinate, and this letter was sent to him too, because he was the deputy chief for war crimes and terrorism. And there were persons there that were up for war crimes. So I considered that he should participate, together with others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ahmet Avdic, is the next one. Let me repeat again, it is the same as Adem Mehmedovic. He was a Bosniak by ethnicity and he was in the crime police and the war crimes section. He was subordinate to Ante Mikulic, so not to me -- indirectly to me but directly to Ante Mikulic. He was his subordinate. Then we come to Josip Vrancic who was a retired policeman whom reactivated or mobilised, in fact, six months beforehand because we thought he was somebody who could help us because of his experience. So he was in the searches section. He wasn't a leader, didn't hold a leadership post in the police force. He had secondary school education and helped out that way. Then we come to Ivan Nekic. He was chief of the crime technicians department. He was subordinate to me, and the crime technicians department had responsibilities towards everybody who was taken to the holding centre for war crimes. They needed to be processed, fingerprints taken and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, that may be an appropriate time for a break. And, Mr. President, I don't know how you wish to deal with the statements, whether you want to take a longer break or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kardum, you have seen your statements as written down and translated into your own language. How much time you think you would need to read through them and to see whether there are any portions which you're unhappy with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are 23 typed-out pages in total. I will do my best to get through them in, let's say, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll then have a break and -- Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are some documents referred to. You may just wish to verify that the documents that are referenced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness -- may I take it that there is no objection against providing the witness with documents -- if reference is made to certain documents, would it be clear for the witness where to find the documents, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. For the witness's reference --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So Mr. Kardum, if you could open up this binder. You will see that there a coloured tab and that's the reference to your first statement which we have extracted and given to you, and then there's one document which is referred to in your first statement. And then you will see there's a pink tab and that's the reference to the second statement. And then if you look at the numbers on the tabs, those numbers correspond to the paragraph numbers in your second statement in which the documents behind the tab are referred to. So if you take tab 10, that will be the documents referred to in paragraph 10 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that clear to you, Mr. Kardum? Mr. Kardum, is the method clear to you, that what you find after tab 8 then it would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did understand that. I don't think there will be any problems there because these were documents that were mostly compiled outside my jurisdiction, so perhaps I will be able to comment on some but not on others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what we invite to you do at this moment is exclusively look at your statements, if there's a need to -- to check with the documents you're talking about, of course, you have them now available. What we would like to know is whether to what extent the statement as put on paper reflects what you said at that time and also whether that is an accurate reflection of what happened at that time. We don't want you to start further explaining all kind of matters. We just first want to know whether your statement is accurate, that this reflects accurately your words and whether it accurately reflects what happened at the time. We will have a break, and we will resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, we asked you to spend your time during the break on reviewing your statements. Could you help us and tell us where you found problems? And may I then perhaps first take you to your March 2004 statement. If would you just take us to the paragraphs where you think something should be amended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I managed to look through the statement, the note, the first one but not the second one. I underlined what I consider was not as I had put it or was not correctly translated. So, if you like, I can go through them one by one or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or depending on what the Prosecutor wants to ask me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we would like to have your statement [B/C/S on English channel]. Still no English on channel 4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I can hear the English [B/C/S on English channel]. Same problem as a minute ago. It could be better by now. Yes. Could you take us -- what is the first paragraph on which you'd like to amend your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first paragraph and the last thing there, I didn't mention that. This reserve senior Sergeant now where it says "first class," I don't think I said this, "first class." It's not an essential point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just looking at this moment at your 2004 statement. You say the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first paragraph and the last word is what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll read to you what I have in English. "I left the military in 1982 with the rank of reserve senior Sergeant." That's how it reads in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without the first class. In the Croatian version, the last words are "first class."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That at least does not appear in the English, so if there's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So just reserve Sergeant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second paragraph is all right. The third is all right too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... perhaps it was the "senior" which is then translated as -- but we have that on the record. You said the second is all right. The third ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third is all right. The fourth is all right as well. And so is the fifth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take us to the first paragraph which is not all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fifth paragraph is all right. As far as the fifth paragraph goes, when it refers to "... came under Martic's authority." "The Benkovac and Obrovac police station during the first half of 1991, came under Martic's authority or the authority of Martic." So I'd like to refer to the last sentence in paragraph 5. They did not come under the authority of Martic, they were occupied by the rebel Serbs led by Martic. And they were -- the Croats were ethnically cleansed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Almost wholly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then take it to say that they came under Martic's power. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Came under, that would imply that somebody gave it to Martic. But Martic occupied it forcibly, so in a very different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if I understand you well, this ... And if we just add: "... came, due to the occupation --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "-- under the authority of Martic." That is, that it was the consequence of the occupation. Next paragraph in which you would like to make an amendment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next paragraph is paragraph 7. This was the first time that it became clear to the Croats where the JNA stood in this conflict. That's the sentence. It was clear to the Croats quite a long time ago. However, when this aggression was launched with the artillery and the aviation and so on, on two Croatian villages, Krusevo and Jasenica which at the time had a population of about 4.000, there were more dead and wounded and the entire population was expelled and those who were weren't expelled were liquidated, killed later on. So that's it. So it was as a result of that that it became clear to them who the JNA was, through this act committed in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say -- one second. I'm trying to reflect what you said, and could I say: Due to the way in which these villages were taken over, and of course part of what you just said is now also on the record, that you said that this was the artillery and the aviation, but that due to the way in which these villages were taken over, it became once again clear to the Croats where the JNA stood in this conflict. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would add, even the Croats who disbelieved it then came to realize what and who the JNA actually was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it became once again clear to the Croats, even to those who disbelieved it prior to that, where the JNA stood in this conflict. Yes. That is then on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And any further -- next paragraph in which you'd like to make changes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next paragraph I would like to refer to is number 8, in the fourth sentence. "The JNA left their barracks in Zadar peacefully."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA did not peacefully leave their barracks in Zadar but what happened was this. At the time when they left the barracks, I particularly remembered and we all remembered this in Zadar, that the 5th -- it was the 5th of October, 1991, when 46 people were killed in Zadar during an attack of the so-called JNA and rebel Serbs when they reached the outskirts of Zadar and almost entered the town proper. So on that day alone 46 people were killed. I think that I have given you the exact figure but there's a list and testimony of that and of course most of them were civilians. Rockets were used and the cathedral in Zadar was hit from the air. Zadar was targeted from the sea, from the ships, from the air, and from the ground forces, artillery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So not peacefully. Not peacefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I've earlier asked you not to add and further elaborate, but we'll just take out the word "peacefully." They left -- you have now depicted the circumstances as you saw them at the time, the circumstances under which they left but in your statement we just take out at this moment, peacefully. Please proceed. The next --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. The JNA then, along with the massive use of force, left Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They left their barracks in Zadar and it's now on the record that -- your views on the circumstances. The next ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the commander, the direct commander was General Mladic and Momcilo Perisic. Momcilo Perisic from Zadar and General Mladic from the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you now to move to the next portion which you'd like to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 12 is the next one I'd like to deal with. The word "department" is used whereas it should be "section."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same thing with company, the example I gave of company and battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not odjel but odsjek [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Section" is replaced by "department." The next paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14, after the Maslenica operation the Croatian front line moved and we recovered some of our territory. That was our entire territory, in actual fact. So we didn't go into anybody else's territory, somebody else's territory, that should be understood it was all our territory in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I did understand this to be that although you recovered that territory that that was not all of the territory you had at that time lost. Yes? So with this understanding, I don't think -- that it's understood in this way that it doesn't need to be amended or corrected. It is on the record now, yes. Next paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 15 is all right. 16 is all right, 17th is all right. 18th is all right. The 19th, again the department versus section so that should be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just find it. There was also a department for organised crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Department for organised crime -- for general crime. So these are not departments. They're all sections. It should read "section" everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now let me just ... it now reads: "It also had a special section dealing with white-collar crime, fraud and financial crime. There was also was a section for organised crime, an anti-drug section and an anti-terrorist and general crime section which included the crime of murder and other such crimes." So in English now it says "section" several times and that's what you consider to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Section, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, the next paragraph in which you'd like to make ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 20th paragraph. "At the level of the ministry, the decision was made for the crime police to remain at the original police stations as the workload increased in our area as we had to deal with prisoners of war." I don't know where this sentence is coming from. At the level of the ministry. I don't understand this. This is not something that I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- yes. You say the decision was made at the level of the ministry to keep crime police, et cetera. Would you like to take out "the level of the ministry." It then reads: "The decision --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have no idea where it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then it becomes: "The decision was made to keep the crime police at their original police stations as the workload increased." Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just want to make it clear. I could not change what the jurisdiction of the police was. I could not change it from police station to police station. This couldn't even be done by the ministry. We could perhaps change their jurisdictions for a day or two, but that's it. I could not send people from the first police station in Zadar to Knin. This was not something that I had under my powers and of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that you want to further explain, but have your concerns been addressed if we take out "at the level of the ministry"? The line then reading: "The decision was made to keep the crime police at their original police stations as the workload increased in our area," et cetera. Does that meet your concerns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would rephrase that. We could not send policemen from police stations because of an increased workload but we also didn't have the authority to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we couldn't send the policemen who remained in Zadar -- in the area of Zadar because of an increased workload.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say there was an increased workload but even if there would not have been, even then we would not have had the competence to send them somewhere beyond the jurisdiction they were in. Yes. That is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I could not have done that. I could do it for a day or two but I could not issue any sort of official document and assign them to a different police station. I don't think it could be done even by the chief of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay, that's on the record now as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then in the same paragraph: "In Zadar a collection centre for civilians was formed." This was actually a reception centre for civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say "collection centre" should be "reception centre."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reception centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this was something that a civilian organisation actually dealt with. They were in charge of the expelled people or people who were refugees. And I think also the Red Cross had a role in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It reads now: "But that was dealt with by a civilian organisation," and you find that accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So not the police but civilian organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says at this moment. Could you take us to the next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The reception centre for where it says the -- where it says the "collection centre for prisoners of war" it should be the "reception centre for prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So two times the word "collection" is replaced by "reception." Yes. The next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next remark has to do with -- refers to paragraph 34. It says: "A Serb witness called Zivko Borak was able to help me, including some men from the ministry including Marijan Benko and others." At this time Marijan Benko was in charge of this investigation. He had been in Zadar for a month and at this time Ivan Nadj was also in Zadar. Milan Turkalj, the chief of the general crime section -- department, some colleagues from the Zagreb administration, the Split-Dalmatia administration, and Rijeka and Primorje administrations. The point is they were not -- they did not assist me. They were actually leading this project. An assistant minister cannot assist; they can just -- they are actually the ones who lead a project of that type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then make it: "During the course of the investigation, a number of other police representatives conducted the investigation, including ..." Yes, that's on the record. Next paragraph, please, where you'd like to make a change.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 35. I don't have any special remarks there except some clarifications if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know on what point you'd like to clarify anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, I will clarify certain things. Otherwise, I don't have any remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So in itself, it is not inaccurate what is said here, and does reflect what you said. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph in which would you like to make a correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 36, the last sentence. "If we found a freshly killed body in September 1995, it would clearly be a murder; but if we found a decomposed body, it could be either a murder or the result of the combat activities." I would like to add here also death of natural causes, suicide and similar. Because there were a lot of instances where older people died of natural causes, which was, of course, something that was also established after an autopsy, and there were also suicides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that you like to add in 36 that apart from murder and combat activities there are another -- there are causes of death which you did not want to exclude here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Natural causes, suicide and so on. I even have some examples with me, and you can see that these numbers were not insignificant. There were quite a number of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at least your statement has been completed or has been clarified in this respect. The next paragraph, in which you would like to make --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 38. It says: "The army which had just won the war was very cocky and confident and difficult to deal with." The interpretation is a bit clumsy and I certainly did not use the word "cocky." At this time, the Croatian army was proud. The boys were aware that they accomplished a great feat and they were happy, proud, not cocky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... proud and happy and confident and difficult to deal with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were proud of their accomplishment, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next paragraph in which you'd like to make a change.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 39 is all right. 44, the last sentence: "I know that some bodies collected by the civilian protection were collected from outside of Croatia, from over the border in Bosnia." This referred mainly to the border area with Bosnia and Herzegovina. The people from the civilian protection were not certain whether a village belonged to Croatia or to Bosnia, so they collected bodies that they found in houses or, I don't know where else, so this -- the number of such cases was, I think, 12. Some of them were civilian; some were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says -- some --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were mainly decomposed bodes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some were collected just at the other side of the border, which means not far away but -- yes. Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right. There is specific mention of the place where this happened, the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell us where your next correction would be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 47. My first visit to Knin, and then in the third line from the bottom it says: "After Drnis I could see destroyed houses, although I could not say when they were destroyed." I just want to make sure that we understand each other. I don't know if this was in 1991, 1992, 1993, or 1994, but certainly they had been destroyed before Operation Storm because these were Croatian areas that were under Serbian control until Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say from the fact that these were Croatian areas --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Serbian control until Operation Storm, you concluded that they were not destroyed during Operation Storm. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, clearly. Because it's obvious if a house was destroyed one, two, or three years before or just -- just destroyed, you can tell. Paragraph 51, the second sentence: "I, as chief of the crime police, should have been told about that crime but somebody in authority obviously decided ..." This is not true. Somebody in authority, I did not say this portion "in authority." Somebody did say it but it has nothing to do with authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it now reads: "... have been told about the crime but somebody obviously decided that we were not to be involved." And we took out "in authority." The next --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was supposed -- I should have been told about the crime but obviously somebody had decided that this should not be done. I assumed that somebody made that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have no actual knowledge of who made such a decision, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take to us your next correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is as far as I managed to get. I didn't get to review the rest. I can do it during the next break, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now let me -- you said this is until where, is that including the whole of paragraph 51?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not yet 52.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I ask you already now, and I will later put the same question to you in respect of the paragraphs that you have then reviewed, do we now understand that with the corrections you just made that the paragraphs 1, 2, and up to and including 51 of your 2004 statement reflects what you said at that time, that it accurately reflects what you said with these corrections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You gave that statement to the best of your recollection, as reflecting the truth? And that if the same questions would you put to you today, that you would answer in the same sense.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maybe I would have clarified some matters if they weren't clear enough or totally explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We actually would like you to do the remainder of the work, not only the 2004 statement but also the 2007 statement, if possible during the next break. Mr. Margetts, I did what perhaps I could have left in your hands as well. I hope you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
