utterances.text: Not at all. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, prior to reviewing the statement and prior to the break we were addressing the issue of the prisoner of war centre in Zadar. And what I'd like to do is I'd like to show you a file of one of the people who appeared on the list of persons in the centre that we've already reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please bring up on the screen 65 ter 5284.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, what you see there is a picture of one of the detainees on the right-hand side of the screen. A gentleman by the name of Jovan Rokvic, and his date of birth, et cetera, is recorded and you will see that there's a reference to a Z-1 form at the top of that page there. Were there prescribed forms that your investigators were to fill out upon the admission of detainees in the collection centres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please move on, to the third page of the B/C/S and to the third page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Kardum, you'll see that there's a form at the top there and that's a Z-2 form. Again, was that a prescribed form that the investigators were required to fill out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if we could now move on to page 6 of the English, or, in fact, to page 7 of the English. And that is 206105484 of the B/C/S, or page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now if we could look at the signature on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If we could look, Mr. Registrar, at the bottom of the B/C/S there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Is that your signature there, Mr. Kardum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my signature as typed, but the signature itself is not my own. Somebody signed this for me, but that person was authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if we could now just move through, Mr. Registrar, the remaining pages so that Mr. Kardum can see that the next page is an Official Note. And move through to the next page and just leaf through the pages, if we could. And to the following page. And if we can just stop there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you could look at this page here. This is a letter signed by the chief of the crime police Marijan Babic. And it refers to the institution of proceedings against Jovan Rokvic. And the crime is under Article 231 of the Criminal Code. Now I may be stretching your memory, and there may have been changes since then, but do you recall what Article of the Code -- well, not what Article but what crime in the code Article 231 refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't recall with precision but these are offences similar to armed rebellion. It is not war crimes. This is not a perpetrator of a war crime. This man was in some way involved in the armed rebellion. I can see here that this man was born in 1922, so in 1991 he was probably 60-something old and these men were usually involved in armed village groups that manned some barricade, stopped civilians from moving on so on. So this referred to 1991/1992, as far as can I see. And also this report was submitted by the crime police of the military police, while we, during our investigation, established that he participated in all this. We returned him to the civilian reception centre and then it was further processed. Very often crime reports were not collated with the -- between the civilian and the military police. If you had to issue a warrant for arrest, this could not be done by the military police. It had to be conducted by the -- or issued by the crime police, the civilian police. But these people were not -- we had no access to them. They were not accessible to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, just to be specific, and you've described generally what Article 231 referred to, would it be correct to refer to that Article as being the offence of a threat to territorial integrity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You could put it that way. This Article does exist of the Criminal Code. I don't remember it word for word but it is quite clear in what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, does this file, the -- we saw a lengthy list of the detainees, but for each of the detainees was a similar type of processing engaged in by your criminal police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. He wasn't a detainee or a prisoner. He had -- it was somebody who had just been taken into custody. So the police couldn't incarcerate anybody or -- all they could do was hold them in detention for 48 hours, I think, in custody for 48 hours, on remand, and after that, they would have to ask the investigating judge to prolong custody. So the police could not incarcerate anybody so it wasn't a detainee -- or detain anyone, so it wasn't a detainee or a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In respect of this individual who was in the reception centre, is this an example of the processing that each of the persons in the centre were -- were subject to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean. I'm not quite clear on the question. But can I explain what the general procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, if he could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt my colleague. Just the use of the terminology, I think we've had evidence now that there were two reception centres. Are we talking about the POW reception centre and what the procedures were there or are we talking about the civilian? And from what I understand from the testimony, this individual was in both the civilian and the POW centre, so if we could just for the witness clarify which centre we're talking about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, if you would do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We're talking about the reception centre where the prisoners of war were present, and I'd just like you to explain to the Court, as you were about to do, the process, the -- the forms that were filled out, the interviews, Official Notes, and the processing that was engaged in, in respect of each of the persons who were in the centre, and whether or not this example that we've looked at is a typical example. Mr. Kardum, I note you've got some pages there. If you could just possibly put them in the briefcase. And what is that page that you have extracted? I wonder if I could have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's my own document, not yours. I took it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Maybe if that could be presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- the Chamber was not aware that you brought any documents with you. If you want to look at your own documents, would you please ask first or announce that you intend to do that so that permission can be given to you. This is a document which is in B/C/S and, therefore, at this moment I've got no idea -- Could you tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. All I wanted was to help out the Prosecutor so I brought in a copy of the questions that each crime department policeman had when interviewing somebody in the reception centre. It's a sort of form which was a universal questionnaire, if I can put it that way, and it was universal procedure. It was written in the MUP and sent to us, so it's the procedure. When somebody came to a POW reception centre, the particulars of that person were taken, name, surname, name of the father, et cetera, and then a team of physicians would examine the person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and then there was a notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a second. Would you mind that a copy was made of this document. This is the complete document, one page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against that. Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest -- it is a document with nine numbered paragraphs and then one final paragraph, saying "napomena." I suggest that we have it copied, that a copy will be provided to all parties, that the parties will then consider the relevance of the document and to see whether you want to tender that. Madam Usher, do you think that there would be any way of having it copied during this session. Thank you. Could you please focus again, because Mr. Margetts was asking you whether the documents that were prepared as we found them on our screen, Official Notes, questionnaires, et cetera, whether that was typically the paperwork that was made when people had arrived in the prisoners of war collection centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. When the person arrived in the reception centre for POWs, not criminals, but POWs, and that is an essential difference of course in concept and terms, that person was examined by doctors first. And any injuries were noted and recorded, if they were such that they required hospitalisation or hospital treatment, and the priority was to sent these people to a hospital for treatment. So based on that, regardless of the fact that some people had taken part in an armed rebellion were dispatched to hospitals for treatment. I remember some of the names, cases in point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts is not primarily focussing on what you would do with those people who needed medical care. I now do understand that you gave that medical care. Mr. Margetts was asking --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether the type of documents we saw on the screen whether they were typical for processing those who had arrived in the centre for prisoners of war. And I also noticed that there is no medical documentation apparently under these 16 pages, and to that extent, your explanation certainly have assisted that apart from this way of proceeding that if somebody needed medical care that he would receive that. Is that correctly understood? But now, again, is this paperwork, as we find it here, interviews, is that typical for those who arrived -- had arrived in the prisoner of war centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Those are typical documents because one of our priorities was to learn about the distribution of minefields, for instance, for stragglers in Srpska Krajina so-called that were hiding in caves and woods, to learn about the mass graves and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if Mr. Margetts would like to know why you created those documents, he will certainly ask you, yes? Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kardum, my focus is on the file and you've indicated that that is a typical file and that these were the typical documents prepared in respect of the persons in the centre. In respect of each of the individuals detained, how many of your crime policemen were engaged in the interview process of each of the individuals detained -- sorry, I will rephrase that. Of each of the persons who were in the centre, and I withdraw the reference to any -- to them being detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say. But usually one or two persons. I won't exclude the possibility of having three people present, but usually one or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please now proceed and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise but I have to stress something at this point, when you asked about the number of people. So the interview could have been conducted, for example, by someone from the crime police, the civilian police, and pursuant to a separate request, the interview could also be conducted by somebody from the secret police and from the SIS but pursuant to a special request. And then those people -- but the people could not be taken out of the reception centre, if you mean the number of people. So there you have it. So one or two people, and that's my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5276 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, do you recognise your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is my signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could now move to 65 ter 5277.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you will have seen the previous document was the cover page. And this is a report that you've submitted on the treatment of prisoners of war on the 21st of August. Do you recognise that report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to the third page of the English, please, and to the second page of the Croatian. Now, Mr. Kardum, you will see in the last paragraph of the second page there, it -- precisely as you have just described, you recorded that during the criminal processing, the officials used a list of interview questions prepared in advance, that's at the bottom also of the English page 3. And short summaries of all the crimes committed in the period from 1991 up to -- that is the beginning of Operation Storm. Now, if we move on in the Croatian and we go to the fourth page. And if we look just under the heading, conclusion, Mr. Kardum, you'll see that there's a reference to a telegram from the Republic of Croatia MUP. It's the reference number there and it's dated the 4th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I think -- yes, we need to go to another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Oh, apologies. Apologies. Yes, if we could proceed to the bottom of the fifth page in the English. Well, that actually goes over to the sixth page. And you will see, Your Honour, that the reference I was making was to a telegram from the Ministry of the Interior. And that is one of the exhibits on our exhibit list so we'll refer to that another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You can see there, Mr. Kardum, that the telegram was dated the 4th of August and that this report refers to the functioning of the Mocire sport hall until 19th of August, 1995. Do you recall that the prisoner of war facility was operated pursuant to directions from the Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well. I was there every day. I don't know what you wish to contest there or what you're looking for there. What's the meaning of your question? Do you have a question in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, the only question is I just wanted to look at those various components of this report and confirm that this is the report and then my question comes just after the next reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if Mr. Registrar could please now move forward through the table of persons who were processed in the centre. And in the B/C/S we'll get to page 06105015, which is some ten pages on from where we currently are. And in the English that is page 23 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, Mr. Kardum, in that period from the 4th August through to the 19th August, is that correct that you processed 183 persons in the prisoner of war centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct that 183 persons went past the centre. That number of persons were processed but more went through. Some were returned to the civilian reception centre which means that when the police established that those individuals had nothing to do with any previous reports about those individuals or statements made and so on and so forth, then they were released straight away. They were let go, and they went to the reception centre for civilians and they were treated exclusively as civilians there. So this is the number of persons who were processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. The next question I have is, you have just reviewed your statement of 2004 and at paragraph 41 of the statement you will recall that you said that and your men were at that time fully employed at the collection centre according to the instructions from the Ministry of the Interior. That's the 2004 statement at paragraph 41. I'm just trying to understand precisely the engagement of your men in these tasks. And you had 50 to 60 men, you have referred to the number of men that you had. Is it the case that they were all engaged at the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could explain to the Trial Chamber how many men were engaged in the processing of the prisoners of war or, alternatively interviewing other persons. In your statement you indicate that interviews were also conducted of civilians and how otherwise the 50 to 60 men, under your authority, were engaged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they weren't all my men sent to the reception centre for POWs. Life went on. We -- our town was the fifth largest one in Croatia, that is to say, Zadar and we had to cover it, to deal with our regular affairs, go about our daily business. So not everything took place in the reception centre. There were killings, murders in Zadar, for example, there were holdups, robberies, violent crimes and so on, whereas I told you who the 50 and 60 men were. They were crime technicians. For example, in the centre -- well, we covered the reception centre permanently. There were one or two crime technicians permanently in the POW reception centre. Whereas I had a total of 12 of them and we had to work two shifts because we did 12 hours on, 12 hours off. Those were the shifts, which means that in a 24-hour period I had to have four crime technicians out of a total of 12 and the rest were engaged in other affairs, other business. So we didn't only have to cater to the reception centre, we had to deal with our current daily affairs. I don't know if I have succeeded in clarifying the situation. So we were given the reception centre for POWs to take care of and the priority of the crime police was to uncover mass and individual graves where Croats had been buried. There was such a lot of pressure from the public, for example, that we had to find out where their nearest and dearest lay. You might not be interested in that but it is very important to know that during that period we found about 310 Croats who had been killed and buried in different individual and mass grave sites, and we were the protagonists of that work. The crime police had to uncover the whereabouts of those bodies. That was part of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kardum, could you just indicate to the Court that the -- the matters that you were investigating -- in the investigations you were conducting at the prisoner of war reception centre, those matters involved the crimes that had been committed on the territory prior to Operation Storm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before Operation Storm and during Operation Storm, that is to say, those committed on occupied Croatian territory. Some people shot at Zadar and Sibenik. Others -- I see here that there were three people who were accused of war crimes or whatever, I think that's the piece of information here. Just a moment. Article 120 or paragraph 120, whichever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And just for clarification, were any Croatian soldiers held in the reception centre for prisoners of war for crimes that they had committed during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. No, no, no, no, no. There were no Croatian soldiers in that reception centre. They were POWs who were combatants fighting against the Republic of Croatia and amongst them there were 13 Croats as can you see. And I can explain that, how come 13 Croats there. These were people who were born and lived in the territory and under various threats to their families and so on, they were forced into mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And that was mobilisation for which forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The so-called army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the Croats were forcibly mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kardum, if I can bring you now back to your 2004 statement. And at paragraph 47 of your 2004 statement, you refer in the first sentence to your visit to Knin on the 7th, 8th, or 9th of August. And then if I could refer you down to paragraph 49, where you state that you visited the civilian collection centre in Knin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which paragraph did you say? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The first sentence for the purpose of indicating the date at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And just after reading the first paragraph where it refers to 7th, 8th or 9th August, if you could refer then to paragraph 49 where you state that you visited the civilian collection centre in Knin a few days later where three of your crime police were. And if you could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ... we sometimes need additional time to let the interpreters translate everything you say. Perhaps you repeat your question, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'm just interested to ask you do you recall the names of the crime police who were at the collection centre in Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And what were their names and who was the leader of those crime police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their names were Slavko Raspovic, Dejan Klanac and Bozo Razov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And what was their role at the Knin collection centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to make a correction. It wasn't a collection centre; it was a reception centre. And their role was to look after the people and through conversations with them, or interviews, to learn whether any of those people who had arrived there, and people arrived in different ways to the centre, many of them voluntarily, whether they had taken part in an armed rebellion against the Republic of Croatia or had committed some war crime to try and identify such persons, and to escort them to Zadar. Among others, they made up lists of such persons and checked them out in Zadar to see if there were criminal reports filed against these people in Zadar because they weren't able to check that out in Knin. They didn't have the necessary facilities, so they would ask people in Zadar or send faxes to find out, and if they were under an investigation then they would take it further. So that was their only role in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I'm looking at the clock. Mr. Kardum, from your first statement there are still a limited number of six paragraphs to review, and then the other statement is - let me just check - there are 37 paragraphs. How much time do you think you would need to finish the job? Would half an hour do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, already we'll ask Madam Usher to escort you out of the courtroom. I'm sorry to give you homework for the breaks, but it's very much appreciated that you want to cooperate. Madam Usher, could you already escort Mr. Kardum out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It gives the Chamber an opportunity to briefly deal with a procedural matter, because the Chamber would like to make an invitation to the parties regarding the boundaries of Croatian municipalities, or "opcine" in Croatian, as relevant to the indictment. The indictment refers, among others, to Ervenik, Kistanje, Knin, and Orlic municipalities. Its use of the word "municipality" corresponds to how these areas are defined in map 9 of the court map binder. However, map 21 of the binder suggests that the Knin municipality may include all of those areas as administrative subdivisions. Maps 16 through 26 are all similar to map 21 in their interpretation of the term "municipality." The Chamber invites the parties to agree on the correct understanding of the division of Croatian municipalities at the time relevant to the indictment. If Ervenik, Kistanje, et cetera, were in fact municipal subdivisions, then the Chamber also invites the parties to agree on a term that would correctly refer to those. The parties are invited to present their agreement, or, if no agreement is reached, make submissions on the matter by Monday, the 29th of September of 2008. And this concludes the Chamber's invitation to the parties. I take it that after the break it will take us some time to go through the corrections the witness would like to make. I dealt with the matter, because I got the impression that there is a risk that if it is not done in a rather strict way that we might lose time and I hope, but if the party would disagree, that some of my authority would help to proceed. But if there's anything against it, then of course I'd like to know. But I try to do it as transparent as possible. We will have a break, and we resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'd like to make a follow-up exercise with you. Could we start your 2004 statement, paragraph 52 and following.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 55. Your Honour, I would appreciate if you allowed me a few moments to comment on this paragraph, or, rather, on its last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kardum, if it reflects what you said, please let me know. If you think that what it says is not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only partially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then if you tell me to what extent it does and to what extent it does not, but please keep it brief, because the parties will examine you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... I will be very brief. This paragraph only partially reflects what I think so I would like to add on to it. It says here, if you allow me to go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence reads: "I am aware that part of the Serb position was prepared to leave the area from documents that have come to light since and also from statements made by some Serb returnees." Your Honour, in one of my reports I mentioned some figures and now I would like to repeat them. During the occupation, about 1.000 Croatian civilians were killed, about 1.500 Croatian police and military were killed, some 10.000 homes of expelled Croats were destroyed and looted, so that 98 per cent of Croats were expelled from that area and also from the border areas that were under the control of the Croatian authorities, in addition to the -- or because of the daily shelling and so on. Before Operation Storm, there were rumours that Serbs were claiming that if Croats were to come there, they would not remain there. I would like to stress a fact here. The Serb leadership ethnically cleansed the area, the occupied areas of the Republic of Croatia in 1991, 1992 and 1993, but not only then, and also in 1995. This time, they cleansed their own population because there they were unprepared wait for the Croatian authorities facing -- in face of the crimes that they had committed. The same people who had cleansed Croatia of Croatian civilians did the same thing when they cleansed those areas of the Serb population. In the Zadar police administration, we saw that -- we knew that some Serbs had been killed by Serbs because they did not want to flee the Republic of Croatia. Of course, they were misinformed. They were threatened, they were made afraid, and they were told about horrible things that Croats did, all for the purpose of making them move out of that area, whereby they would also justify their own inability to wait for the arrival -- to await the arrival of the Croatian authorities, and to await those authorities, the Croatian authorities to judge them, and this is all that I wanted to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Could you please -- it -- I consider this to be additional evidence rather than an amendment of the statement because it does not contradict; it adds and explains. Nevertheless, I would like you to not to give statements of a general nature but rather focus on to what extent something is not accurate in your statement. The next paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the -- I have no further comments on the first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's move to the 2007 statement. Could you take us to the first paragraph where you'd like to make an amendment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 9 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is stated here that I said the police administrations of Sisak, Moslavina, Karlovac, Lika, Senj, Zadar-Knin, Sibenik, Split-Dalmatia, Knin and Glina, which orders in paragraph number 2 that the chiefs of the police administration are to meet. And I think what was omitted here is a meeting with the commanders of battalions of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, this does not really reflect on me. This has something that has a reference to my chief, but I thought it should be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the order, as you tell us, was that there should be a meeting -- not only with the chiefs of police but that in the meeting the commanders of the battalions of the military police should also participate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please take us to the next parts of your statement where you think a correction is needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add to paragraph 10, but I think I should clarify a bit why we needed to take the measures as required. But if you feel it's not necessary I can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As long as your statement is accurate, if there's any need for further explanations, the parties will ask you for it. The next paragraph in which you feel a correction is needed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 15. It says, "the command headquarters Povratak." They were operational headquarters, not command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the word "command" is replaced by "operational."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next correction would be in what paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next paragraph that needs to be corrected is paragraph 30, the last sentence: "These documents were completed in Zagreb and were not distributed to the police -- the police administration, Zadar-Knin." As far as I know, that's how it was. I've never seen those documents. Maybe someone has received them, but I have never seen those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we add: "But were to my knowledge not distributed to the police in Zadar-Knin." Would that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least not to the chiefs or heads at my level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And were, to your knowledge, not distributed to police authorities of your level in Zadar-Knin. That's on the record. Could you take us to the next --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, I would like to stress once again. I was responsible for two to three per cent of the total number of men at the police administration. So I don't know if my chief, if he had received the document, whether he distributed it to other departments, but I've never seen it. As for the other -- the remaining paragraphs, I have no more comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Then I put the same questions to you as I did before: In relation to paragraph 52 and following of your 2004 statement and the 2007 statement, with the corrections you just made, do they accurately reflect what you said during these interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you give the answers to the questions to the best of your recollection in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you would also give the same answers, perhaps not literally, but you would answer these questions in a similar sense if the same questions would be put to you today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Margetts, I could imagine that you want to tender the 92 ter statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? Mr. Registrar, could you please assign numbers to the 2004 and 2007 statements, the first one 23rd of March, 2004. The other one it says on your list 4th of May but I think it is 4 and 5th of May, Mr. Margetts, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 2004 statement, 65 ter 05273, becomes Exhibit number P896. And the 2007 statement, 65 ter 05274, becomes Exhibit number P897.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These statements, as amended by the witness, are admitted into evidence. I have a very practical question. At some instances it was just replacing one word by another word, very limited. At other instances there was a rather broad explanation or further elaboration on the statement on the answers given during the interviews. Now, I suggest to the parties that where it's simple to add or to replace a word, that we try to get final versions with these additions and that where it was a broader explanation that it can be found on the record that further explanation, further clarification or further elaboration was given by the witness when he gave his testimony. Of course, I would prefer if the parties would agree on a new version of 896 and 897.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're happy to take the initiative of that and send a proposed version to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, just in relation to the exhibits or the documents that were referred to in the statements, we don't have objections to those now that the 92 ter procedure has been complied. If we could have exhibit number for those documents, and that is up to document number 33 in the exhibit list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we do it as we usually do it, that is, that we invite Mr. Registrar to prepare a list so that we have them all -- that numbers are provisionally assigned to these documents and that we then decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if we could proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please bring back 65 ter 5206 and if we could go to the B/C/S page 5. And if, Madam Usher, I could have some assistance. The English of this document is currently on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, we've talked about the various taskings that you had and the report that you submitted in relation to the prisoner of war collection centre. And you'll note and we did in fact note that between the dates of the 5th of August and the 19th of August, 183 people were processed through the centre. And we noted the nature of the investigations that were conducted. Now, these were the people who were involved in that process. And you've indicated to the Court precisely who they were subordinated to and what their role was. My question is: In respect of each of those individuals, how many crime police officers were working with them at the time, and precisely how did that facilitate the processing of 183 people in a 14-day period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. I think I said that one to two persons spoke or interviewed each of these people. I also left the possibility of three persons actually doing the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And so those one to three people, who were they subordinated to? In other words, which of these six named persons received assistance from other crime police members? Or maybe I haven't understood you. Were you saying that in each interview there were one to three people present? If so, how many interviews were conducted at any one time and, therefore, how many investigators in total were present on any one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One to two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So with those six people, were they working with other persons? Did they have any crime police subordinated to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's obviously a misunderstanding here somewhere. Adem Mehmedovic was the commander of the reception centre Mocire. So he was the commander -- the overall commander in the reception centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So let's focus on Adem Mehmedovic and his role as commander of the centre. How many policemen were subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was responsible for the overall situation in the reception centre, the condition of the prisoners of war, their rights, ensuring that they be examined by doctors, that they receive two to three warm meals, that they have showering facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we've dealt with the reception centre and the activities that the persons there were engaged in. What I want to know is: As commander of that holding centre, how many policemen were subordinated to him for the operation of the centre in the period from the 5th to the 19th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the number of persons who actually participated in these interviews? I couldn't tell you just off the top of my head now, but I think that each shift had about 20 men who worked on these duties. 20 crime policemen. The shifts were 12 hours long, so people would work for 12 hours and then they would be off 12 hours and then they would work the next 12 hour, off again. So I was just giving you a ballpark figure. I think there may even have been a schedule of their duties in writing and the names of these men on those lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So those 20 crime policemen, you've described how many would have participated in each interview, between one to three. So would have there been over ten interviews being conducted at any one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Some people had to make sure that these people who were receiving were registered. Most often these were women policemen -- policewomen. So the first segment, the administrative portion would be done by them. Then somebody would have to inform Mrs. Anka Skrgetic who was not on the premises. She was in the office of the chief of the police administration, so she would have to be informed about who was brought in when. Then would be a person who would be a crime technician to take the fingerprints, to take photos of these individuals and so forth. And some men were the ones who interviewed these men, these people, who were brought in by filling out the forms, Z-1 and Z-2, that we mentioned earlier, because I've already said that the primary interest was to find out what the layout of the minefields was, of straggling groups of rebels, armed groups, to find out about war crimes that had been committed in the area, and the graves where the victims had been buried, about the structure of the civilian and police authorities, the judicial organs, and only then would we want to find out if they had participated in the armed rebellion against the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, I mean I'm sorry for concentrating on this and I'm sorry for misunderstanding. You said there would have been -- there were two shifts, 12 hours long and that there were 20 men who worked on these duties and that each shift had about 20 men. So is that a total -- if there's two shifts, each shift had 20 men, is that a total of 40 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the total in a 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And those 40 men, those 40 -- you referred to them as crime policemen, they were subordinated to Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They worked at the centre where Mehmedovic was commander. But as for the criminal investigation itself, I was the person, pursuant to a written order by Mr. Moric, or the minister, I'm not certain, well, I was the person responsible for criminal investigations conducted in that centre, although I was not there -- I was not seated there permanently. So the chief of the crime police department was responsible for the investigations but not the commander of the centre. The criminal investigation was just one segment of the work of the centre itself. There was a lot that needed to be done there. The building had to be secured from outside, the food had to be provided, medical assistance and so on and so forth. I have to reiterate here, I don't know why you insist so much on the reception centre but I would like to stress that no one was killed in this centre, no one passed -- no one died, no one --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- no one suffered any injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there is no insistence by Mr. Margetts on anything else at this moment as to how many people who were employed there. That's what Mr. Margetts is asking you about and you apparently are -- it looks even a bit as a kind of a defence against allegations that were never made. So therefore there is no need to do that. Could I ask you one additional question. You said on the 24 hours it was 40 police officers involved in -- in two shifts of each 20 men. These 40 were among the 50 to 60 that were subordinated to you. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Plus ten men who were added from Rijeka. They came from the coastal district and another man that came from the Istria district. He had previously lived in Zadar so he knew the conditions prevailing there. And some ten were from my crime police department. 30 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not ten. 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So it's fair to say, and just following on from His Honour's question, it's fair to say that a large proportion of your police were engaged in the work of the prisoner of war centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. During those 14 days, yes, almost half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, during those first 14 days, 183 men were processed. Can you assist the Trial Chamber and inform them how many men were processed in all in the collection centres until their closure, which I understand was around November 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why November 1995? Why do you mention that date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... a reference to the record of November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. The basis for the reference to November 1995 was a report that I have on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But I'm more than happy to withdraw that reference and ask the witness himself what date would he say that the centre was closed and also if he could then answer the second question as well, that is, how many persons were processed up until that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm clear on what you're alluding to but let me put it this way. The centre was closed at the time that you find in writing. That is to say, what date did we say? The 20th of -- well, my special report to MUP with the figure of 183 there mentions the date. I think it was the 28th, in fact. On the 16th -- or, rather, the 20th of August. 20th of August. It's the report to the ministry about closing the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, just -- the first document that I -- one of the first documents that I showed you today was this list of persons who were in the prisoner of war camp and that list continued on until November 19 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Your Honours, I don't allow for the word "camp" to be used. Well, "logor" in the B/C/S, it was a collection centre for prisoners of war, not a camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With full facilities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what you call a camp, I call that and I think it was a detention centre. It is, however, not up to you to tell what language is allowed or not. But it is now clear on the record that you fundamentally disagree with Mr. Margetts on the way in which he qualified the facility he is putting questions about. Mr. Margetts, I do not know whether -- I have not looked in the English, as a matter of fact, what word you used. We all know what we're talking about and what the witness called a reception centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't a "logor," camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. In the reception centre, Mr. Kardum, there were a number of persons and we saw a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if Mr. Registrar could please bring up 65 ter 5278 again. And, Mr. Registrar, if you could please go to 06104954 which should be page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you look down to the last entry you will see that there is an entry that has the date of the person being released, which is the 23rd of November, 1995. And so would you agree that there were prisoners of war being processed up until the 23 -- 23rd of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to explain this. The centre for prisoners of war was closed on the date it says so. That is to say, the 20th of August, 1995. Because during those days very few POWs arrived, one a day or not at all, and so we had to let the Jazine sports hall go and return it to the owner. Now, all the individuals who were brought in later on were people who were brought in from the forests and woods, caught bearing arms and they surrendered themselves to the Croatia police in the subsequent period. And then they weren't taken to that collection centre at all but they were taken to the police administration building where -- well, have you the dates when they were released too. Either on the same day, after they had been processed or the very next day. So they were either set free straight away or sent on for further processing to the respective courts, so the centre really wasn't functioning on the date when the special report was sent out because it was closed. The last person that handed themselves over is not on the list. In 1997, for example, I think it was 1997, that was the last time a person surrendered to the Croatian police and that surrender went through me in actual fact. His name was Sovijetko Popovic, that's his name and surname, and he was from a place called Mokro Polje. We knew that he was in hiding somewhere in the area but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you explained that the reception centre was closed at the date you mentioned but that some other people who turned themselves in were processed at a later stage. We do not have, at this moment at least -- unless Mr. Margetts would like to know further details about who and at what day and for what purpose arrived. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, if you could please display 65 ter 5030. And this is a report from Ivica Cetina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, this is the reference and you'll see it under the name Mirko Kljajic in the second section. And Ivica Cetina says that by 27 November 1995, a total of 277 individuals were admitted to the holding centre for prisoners of war and 277 were released and he gives the details of that. So after the 19th of August and prior to the 27th of November, would you agree with me that 94 people were processed by the Ministry of the Interior as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But not in that particular reception centre. They were processed within the police administration, not as POWs but as the perpetrators of certain crimes against the Republic of Croatia or in areas where international rights and rules applied --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- because the centre wasn't operational at that time. It had already been closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum, for that clarification. And in respect of those 94 persons, can you indicate how many of your crime police were involved in the processing of those persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, fewer. Just four or five were working at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could now move on to 65 ter 5020.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you will see on the first page there, this is a report to the Ministry of the Interior. It's dated the 6th of August. And there's a list of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if we move to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You will see that this is from Ivica Cetina and in the final paragraph he says that as at the 6th of August there are 135 elderly people and children in the holding centre. And then he says that Ivka Babic, at the request of her son, was housed at his home, and Ruzica Zarkovic, at the request of her son, was housed at his home. Can you confirm that this is a reference to the civilians held in the civilian reception centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the centre for prisoners of war, that reception centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No. I mean the -- the location where the civilians were -- were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could be of assistance, I think the problem may be the use of the word "held" in the first question. "Held" connotes some form of detention. That might where the confusion is coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any confusion there, this is -- I'm just asking you: We've seen the distinction between the prisoner of war centre and the civilian centre and I just want to know whether this is a reference to the persons that were held at the civilian centre -- sorry, this is a reference to the persons present at the civilian centre on the 6th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that that is so. I haven't got the list now. But I assume they were civilians who were in the reception centre for civilians on the 6th of August, 1995. If we want further information I can see that Babic here, Sime Babic, and so on, a Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why you want me to comment when the signature is Ivica Cetina. If I can be of assistance, I will be glad to assist but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You can be and you are being, and I thank you for that. Now was there an order from the Ministry of the Interior in relation to the conditions or the circumstances in which persons could be released from the civilian centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And what was that order and what were the conditions for the release of persons from the civilian centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no conditions. The only condition was that the person -- well, usually they were ill persons or infirm persons or elderly persons. And already on the 5th - that is the 5th of August, I mean - the deputy minister [indiscernible] sent to all the police department -- to the police administrations -- well, he said that any relatives capable of looking after these people could take them over without any conditions. All they needed was to leave their address and telephone number if they had them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for the interruption. I'm looking at the transcript at page 81, line 21. The witness made a reference -- I believe the name is not properly recorded, and importantly for us, the witness made a reference to that person's ethnicity which was not picked up on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I obviously thank my learned friend for picking up these matters, but I would prefer if the witness would be allowed to finish their answer and the corrections could be made at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I thought he was finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, at that very moment, interrupted the witness when he was answering a question. I do not blame you for that, because it may well have been beyond what you asked him. But let's -- let's try to see. When you made a reference to -- apparently on the basis of this document of a person by the name Babic, did you refer to the ethnicity of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatian. And the other person was of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the other person was who? Because you referred to Sime Babic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Ivka Babic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you refer to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the other one was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... whose name you saw in the document and by mistake it appears on the transcript as Sime Babic but you referred to Ivka Babic, and you said that that was a person of Croatian nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Ruzica Zarkovic, she was a Serb from a place called Jagodnja, as you can see from this document. If that is at all important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just try to have on the record what you apparently have said before. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have D462 presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, in the course of your previous answer, you referred to an order from Zdravko Zidovec, and if we could scan down, Mr. Registrar, on the B/C/S version. Is this the order you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you can see in this order there is no reference to the state of health of the individual as being a determinant as to whether they were to be picked up by their family is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I know -- I personally know that many of those people ended up in hospital. Some of them even died in hospital, in Zadar. Usually elderly and infirm people, people suffering from mental illness. So people who didn't have anybody to look after them and couldn't look after themselves. That was the case for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, apparently you want to draw attention to the first page in English instead of the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could go back to the first page and if we go down it's the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear to me and the witness, of course, has seen the whole of the document since it is a one-page document for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5028 presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, if you can see this, this is a document from the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons. And you'll the reference at the bottom, the note, it says: "Between 5 August and today," and the date's the 7th of September, 1995, "there have been 596 civilians that passed through the centre for providing care," and you will read on another part went back to their homes or to relatives and consistent with what you -- what your recent answer and part were hospitalised. Is that consistent with your understanding of how many civilians had passed through the centre in Knin between the 5th of August and the 7th of September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very bad copy of this document and I think it's a document from the government of Croatia, as far as I can see. I'm looking at it for the first time. I have never seen it before. I can't even read what it actually says because the copy is such a poor one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well -- the bottom there, there's a reference to the number, there's the note at the bottom, you can see the dark letters below the table which say "note." At the end of that line there is a reference to 596. And so my question is, regardless of whether all words are clear, is it the case, is it consistent with your knowledge that 596 civilians passed through the Knin centre between 5th of August, 1995, and 7th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't comment. Quite a number did go through the centre in Knin. Now, where does this date, the 7th of September come from? I don't think it was operational at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the top of the document above the heading, below the title. You will see Zagreb, 7 September 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the 7th of September, that's the 7th of the 9th month. So this report was written in Zagreb, Sisak, Knin, Zadar, Sibenik, Split, Gospic, et cetera, mentioned. And then a note at the bottom and I see a figure there, 595 or 596. It is not very clear, rather illegible. But that is not our information. It is information from the civilian services, not data worked out on the basis of the information provided by MUP or whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the table, you will see on the left-hand column there are specifications as to where the civilians left to. It states on the top row how many people were in the centres and then it refers to how many of them left and where they left to. In regard to Zadar, you see that the total number is the number at the bottom, which is four columns on, on the bottom row, 926 persons. And you see that 543 of them left to relatives or friends.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This copy is really illegible. Do you have another copy? Because I just can't see that here. Now it's been enlarged, but I can't see what it actually says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It may assist if I hand to you a -- a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a rather a poor copy but better than the last one so I can make something out. But go ahead, I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So my question is: Is that right that nearly all of the people who, up until the 7th of September, had left the facility had left -- had left and gone with relatives or friends, apart, of course, from those who had died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't put it that way. As far as I know, many people returned to their homes. As far as Zadar is concerned, many people returned to their homes. For instance, I know full well that from my particular place, well, the place where I was born, that is, people were taken to the reception centre in Zadar and my late father, among others, took in 12 of those people on the 12th of August, 1995. He took them to his own house in Zadar first and then afterwards he took them to their own homes in Nunic, where they were actually from. And all of them remained in Nunic, went on living in Nunic. Some of them died later. Of course they died a natural death. Others are still alive and live in their own homes up there. I even have a list of those people here. It's on me and if you wish me to provide it to the Court, I will be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, I'm wondering either there was something -- you asked the witness whether it's true that from Zadar that a large number left to relatives and friends. Now the witness explains that, he said, well, most of them went home. Now the one doesn't contradict the other. It is totally unclear to me whether there is any suggestion in your question that leaving or left to relatives or friends would mean that you would not go home, or, on the contrary, that would you go home. That is unclear. Now, you let the witness explain in quite some detail, but it is not clear to me what you're seeking to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I allowed him to explain in some detail. His explanation, I thought, was not entirely relevant to the question. And in fact, there is the issue of the extent of the orders that we've seen and the manner in which these people were dealt with. And without elaborating any further, there is some consistency between those two, the order and the actuality on the territory. So that's effectively the extent to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you are seeking to establish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- what we sought to establish, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock and I establish that it's 7.00. That's -- Then, Mr. Kardum, we'll have to finish for the day, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow because we will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. We adjourn, and we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 23rd of September, 9.00, in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
